claims.text: The initial FeCoNiMnCu alloy is fully disordered and face-centered cubic.
The initial FeCoNiMnCu alloy is soft magnetic with coercive field below 100 Oe.
The intervention is to introduce approximately 50 at.% Pt by replacing one constituent element.
Pt substitution under suitable thermal processing will induce low-symmetry L10 chemical ordering.
Pt substitution will enhance lattice distortion in the alloy.
The treatment will form nanoscale L10-ordered precipitates.
Nanoscale L10-ordered precipitates and their associated lattice distortions will act as domain-wall pinning sites.
Platinum-induced symmetry reduction will enhance magnetocrystalline anisotropy.
Increased magnetocrystalline anisotropy will elevate domain-wall pinning resistance.
Elevated domain-wall pinning resistance will increase the measured coercive field.
The Pt-substituted alloy will have a significantly higher coercive field than identically processed Pt-free FeCoNiMnCu.
The coercive field may move from below 100 Oe toward several hundred Oe.
Coercivity in high-entropy alloys is strongly influenced by microstructure and fabrication conditions.
The coercivity increase is expected only when processing produces the desired low-symmetry L10 ordering.
Insufficient thermal treatment or kinetic constraints may prevent L10 ordering and therefore prevent the coercivity increase.
The magnitude of the coercivity increase may depend on Pt content, processing conditions, and the volume fraction and distribution of L10 regions.
In the cited HEA observations, grain and twin boundaries pin domain walls more strongly than coherent nanoscale L12 precipitates.

contradictions.description: The boundary states that failure to form L10 ordering may prevent the coercivity increase and places the claim outside its intended conditions, whereas the falsification rule says absence of L10 ordering itself falsifies the hypothesis. Failure to realize the required mediator is not a decisive test of the conditional coercivity claim.
